gloss: A program you run on a phone, tablet, or computer.
examples: I downloaded a banking *app* last night.
There are too many *apps* on my phone.
The weather *app* says it's going to rain.

gloss: A set of instructions that tells a computer what to do.
examples: He wrote a small *program* to sort the files.
Some of these *programs* won't run on my old laptop.
The *program* crashed as soon as I opened it.
contrast: American spelling is *program*; British English writes *programme* for a TV show or a plan, but *program* for software.

gloss: The program you use to look at pages on the internet.
examples: Open your *browser* and go to the site.
Most *browsers* will warn you about that page.
My *browser* keeps freezing when I have too many tabs open.

gloss: A set of connected pages on the internet kept in one place.
examples: Their *website* is down again.
I compared prices on three different *websites*.
You can book the whole trip on the airline's *website*.

gloss: The worldwide network that connects computers to each other.
examples: The *internet* went out during the storm.
She found the recipe on the *internet*.
We have no *internet* at the cabin.

gloss: A powerful computer that stores files or runs services for other computers.
examples: The *server* went down for about an hour.
All the photos are backed up on our *servers*.
IT is moving the database to a new *server* this weekend.

gloss: A group of computers or devices connected so they can share information.
examples: The office *network* is running slowly today.
Don't join public *networks* without a VPN.
Our printer is on the same *network* as the laptops.

gloss: A link that lets one device exchange information with another.
examples: My *connection* keeps dropping during video calls.
Hotel *connections* are usually pretty slow.
Check your *connection* before you blame the app.

gloss: A wave or pulse that carries information to a phone, radio, or other device.
examples: There's no *signal* out here in the canyon.
The *signal* gets weak in the basement.
Cell *signals* are much better since they put up the new tower.

gloss: The amount of data a connection can carry in a given time.
examples: Streaming in 4K eats a lot of *bandwidth*.
We don't have enough *bandwidth* for four people working from home.
The video call is using most of our *bandwidth*.

gloss: A fast, always-on internet connection.
examples: *Broadband* still hasn't reached a lot of rural counties.
We pay sixty dollars a month for *broadband*.
You'll need *broadband* to work from home.

gloss: A place or a device that gives nearby phones and laptops internet access.
examples: I turned my phone into a *hotspot* so we could work on the train.
The airport has free *hotspots* near every gate.
The coffee shop's *hotspot* needs a password.

gloss: The name that identifies a website, like the part after the www.
examples: We bought the *domain* before we even had a logo.
Short *domains* are almost all taken.
The *domain* expires next March, so renew it.

gloss: A word or image you click to go to another page or file.
examples: Just send me the *link*.
Half the *links* on that page are broken.
Don't click a *link* from an email you weren't expecting.

gloss: One screen of content on a website.
examples: The *page* takes forever to load.
I bookmarked a few *pages* about the topic.
Scroll to the bottom of the *page* and hit Submit.

gloss: A saved link that lets you return to a page quickly.
examples: Save it as a *bookmark* so you don't lose it.
My *bookmarks* are a complete mess.
I have a *bookmark* for the company intranet.

gloss: A website where someone posts articles or diary entries regularly.
examples: She started a cooking *blog* during the pandemic.
A couple of tech *blogs* covered the story.
His *blog* gets about ten thousand readers a month.

gloss: A system or service that other software and users are built around.
examples: The video *platform* changed its rules again.
We publish on three different *platforms*.
It's the biggest *platform* for freelance work.

gloss: The stream of new posts or updates a site shows you.
examples: My *feed* is nothing but ads lately.
I muted a few accounts to clean up my *feeds*.
Her post showed up at the top of my *feed*.

gloss: The page that holds your name, photo, and details on a site.
examples: Update your *profile* with the new job title.
A lot of these *profiles* are fake.
I couldn't find her *profile* anywhere.

gloss: A small picture or figure that stands for you online.
examples: Pick an *avatar* for your account.
Their *avatars* all look like cartoon animals.
He still uses a photo of his dog as his *avatar*.

gloss: The name you type to identify yourself to a computer system.
examples: I forgot my *username* for that site.
*Usernames* have to be at least six characters.
Your *username* is your work email address.

gloss: A secret word or string that lets you into an account.
examples: Change your *password* every few months.
Don't write your *passwords* on a sticky note.
The *password* has to include a number.

gloss: The act of signing in, or the name and password you use to do it.
examples: The *login* failed three times in a row.
We issue *logins* to new hires on their first day.
Use your company *login* to get into the system.
contrast: One word as a noun (*a login*), two words as a verb (*log in to the system*). Same for *log out* and *a logout*.

gloss: A person who uses a computer, program, or service.
examples: The app has about two million *users*.
Every *user* gets ten gigabytes of free storage.
*Users* complained about the new layout right away.

gloss: Someone who pays for or signs up to receive a service regularly.
examples: The channel passed a million *subscribers* last week.
*Subscribers* get the newsletter a day early.
She's a *subscriber* to three streaming services.

gloss: Someone who has chosen to see another person's posts online.
examples: He gained ten thousand *followers* in a month.
Most of her *followers* are from overseas.
One *follower* pointed out the typo right away.

gloss: A short message a device shows to tell you something has happened.
examples: I turned off *notifications* for that group chat.
A *notification* popped up in the middle of my presentation.
You'll get a *notification* when the package ships.

gloss: A warning message sent to tell you about something important.
examples: I set up an *alert* for that word on my phone.
The bank sends *alerts* for any charge over a hundred dollars.
A weather *alert* woke everybody up at two in the morning.

gloss: Unwanted email or messages sent out in huge numbers.
examples: My inbox is full of *spam*.
That message got filtered as *spam*.
We get less *spam* since they updated the filter.

gloss: A tiny picture used in messages to show a feeling or thing.
examples: He answered with a thumbs-up *emoji*.
She uses way too many *emojis*.
There's an *emoji* for almost everything now.
contrast: Two syllables in the middle: ih-MOH-jee, not "ee-mo-JYE." The usual American plural is *emojis*.

gloss: A word after a # sign used to label a post.
examples: The *hashtag* was trending all afternoon.
Don't put fifteen *hashtags* on one photo.
They made up a *hashtag* for the conference.

gloss: A funny image or phrase that spreads quickly online.
examples: That *meme* was everywhere last summer.
Half the *memes* he posts are ten years old.
Somebody turned the press conference into a *meme*.
contrast: One syllable, rhyming with *seem*. Not "MAY-may" or "MEE-mee."

gloss: A photo you take of yourself, usually with a phone.
examples: She took a *selfie* in front of the fountain.
My camera roll is nothing but *selfies*.
He posted a *selfie* from the summit.

gloss: A conversation typed back and forth in real time online.
examples: Ask the question in the *chat*.
I have about nine group *chats* going.
The support *chat* connected me to a real person.

gloss: A recorded spoken message left for someone who didn't answer.
examples: I left you a *voicemail* this morning.
He never checks his *voicemails*.
Her *voicemail* was four minutes long.

gloss: The sound a phone makes when someone calls.
examples: That *ringtone* drives me crazy.
You can download new *ringtones* for free.
I set a special *ringtone* for my mom.

gloss: An audio show you download or stream in episodes.
examples: I listen to a history *podcast* on my commute.
There are *podcasts* about absolutely everything.
Their *podcast* comes out every Tuesday.

gloss: A saved list of songs or videos played one after another.
examples: She made a *playlist* for the road trip.
My workout *playlists* are all from 2015.
Add that song to the *playlist*.

gloss: Playing video or music straight from the internet instead of downloading it.
examples: *Streaming* has pretty much replaced cable.
The *streaming* kept stopping to buffer.
We spend more on *streaming* than we ever did on movies.

gloss: A file copied from the internet onto your device.
examples: The *download* is taking forever.
Clear out your *downloads* folder once in a while.
The app has over a billion *downloads*.
contrast: As a noun the stress is on the first syllable, DOWN-lohd; as a verb it moves back: down-LOHD the file.

gloss: A file sent from your device to the internet.
examples: The *upload* failed halfway through.
Video *uploads* are limited to two gigabytes.
Wait for the *upload* to finish before you close the tab.

gloss: A newer or better version of something you already have.
examples: The memory *upgrade* made a huge difference.
Both *upgrades* are free for existing customers.
I'm due for a phone *upgrade* in June.
contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (UP-grayd); the verb takes it on the second (up-GRAYD).

gloss: One particular form of a program or document among several.
examples: Which *version* of the app are you running?
Older *versions* don't support this file type.
The new *version* fixed the crash.

gloss: Something a product can do, offered as part of it.
examples: The best *feature* is the offline mode.
They added three new *features* in this release.
That *feature* is only in the paid plan.

gloss: The part of a program you see and interact with.
examples: The *interface* is clean and easy to learn.
Their *interfaces* look the same on the phone and the web.
A confusing *interface* will cost you customers.

gloss: A list of choices a program shows you to pick from.
examples: Open the *menu* in the top right corner.
The settings are buried three *menus* deep.
Pick Export from the File *menu*.

gloss: A small picture on a screen that stands for a file or program.
examples: Double-click the *icon* on your desktop.
The *icons* are too small to see on this monitor.
There's a little gear *icon* for settings.

gloss: The moving mark on a screen that shows where you are typing or pointing.
examples: The *cursor* froze in the middle of the screen.
You can make *cursors* bigger in the accessibility settings.
Put the *cursor* at the end of the line.

gloss: A quick key combination or link that saves you steps.
examples: There's a keyboard *shortcut* for that.
He knows every *shortcut* in the program.
I made a *shortcut* to the folder on my desktop.

gloss: A small piece of software that adds a feature to a bigger program.
examples: Install the *plugin* and restart the browser.
Too many *plugins* will slow the site down.
There's a *plugin* that does the formatting for you.

gloss: An add-on that gives a browser or program extra abilities.
examples: I use an ad-blocking *extension*.
Some *extensions* can read everything you type.
The *extension* stopped working after the update.

gloss: The way things are arranged on a page or screen.
examples: The new *layout* is much easier to read.
They tested four different *layouts*.
The *layout* falls apart on a narrow screen.

gloss: A set of letters and numbers in one particular design.
examples: Pick a *font* that's easy to read.
I have hundreds of *fonts* installed.
The *font* is too small for a slide.

gloss: The temporary place a computer keeps whatever you last copied.
examples: The link is already on your *clipboard*.
Phones and computers keep separate *clipboards*.
Copying the password put it on the *clipboard*.

gloss: A picture of whatever is on your screen at that moment.
examples: Send me a *screenshot* of the error.
I took a few *screenshots* for the bug report.
The *screenshot* was too blurry to read.

gloss: A small version of an image used as a preview.
examples: Click the *thumbnail* to see the full photo.
The *thumbnails* load before the video does.
A good *thumbnail* gets more clicks.
contrast: The *b* is silent: THUM-nayl, the same *thumb* sound as in the finger.

gloss: Sound that has been recorded or is being sent electronically.
examples: The *audio* cut out about halfway through.
The video is fine but the *audio* is terrible.
Can everyone hear the *audio*?

gloss: A picture stored or shown on a screen.
examples: The *image* is too big to email.
Compress the *images* before you upload them.
Right-click the *image* and save it.

gloss: One of the tiny dots that make up a picture on a screen.
examples: Zoom in far enough and you can see every *pixel*.
The screen is about two million *pixels*.
There's a dead *pixel* in the corner of my monitor.

gloss: How much detail a screen or image holds, counted in pixels.
examples: Shoot it at the highest *resolution* you can.
The two monitors run at different *resolutions*.
Low *resolution* looks awful on a big TV.

gloss: The pictures and visual effects a computer produces.
examples: The *graphics* in that game are stunning.
You'll need a better card if you want smooth *graphics*.
The *graphics* look dated now.

gloss: Protection of computers and data from theft or damage.
examples: The bank spends a fortune on *security*.
Weak passwords are a *security* problem.
*Security* is everybody's job, not just IT's.

gloss: The right to keep your personal information from being seen or shared.
examples: Read the *privacy* policy before you sign up.
People care a lot more about *privacy* than they used to.
The app collects data with no regard for *privacy*.
contrast: American PRY-vuh-see; British speakers usually say PRIV-uh-see with a short *i*.

gloss: Software or hardware that blocks unwanted traffic into a network.
examples: The *firewall* is blocking that port.
Corporate *firewalls* won't let you reach the site.
Turn the *firewall* back on when you're done testing.

gloss: The scrambling of data so that only the right person can read it.
examples: The messages use end-to-end *encryption*.
Without *encryption*, anyone on the network can read it.
*Encryption* is on by default now.

gloss: Someone who breaks into computer systems.
examples: A *hacker* got into the payroll system.
*Hackers* stole millions of customer records.
The company hired a *hacker* to test its defenses.

gloss: Software written to damage a computer or steal from it.
examples: The laptop is full of *malware*.
That download turned out to be *malware*.
Most *malware* comes in through email attachments.

gloss: A program that finds and removes harmful software.
examples: Run the *antivirus* before you open that file.
Free *antiviruses* are good enough for most people.
My *antivirus* flagged the installer.

gloss: Tricking people into giving up passwords or card numbers with fake messages.
examples: That email is *phishing* — don't click anything.
The company runs *phishing* tests on its own staff.
*Phishing* still causes most break-ins.
contrast: Pronounced exactly like *fishing*; only the spelling differs.

gloss: A program that runs automatically, often pretending to be a person.
examples: A *bot* answers the first message on their support line.
Half the accounts liking that post are *bots*.
The *bot* books the tickets the second they go on sale.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The written instructions that make up a computer program.
examples: She writes *code* eight hours a day.
There's a lot of old *code* nobody understands anymore.
The bug was three lines of *code*.

gloss: A step-by-step method a computer follows to solve a problem.
examples: The *algorithm* decides what shows up in your feed.
Their sorting *algorithms* are open source.
Nobody outside the company knows how the *algorithm* works.
contrast: Four syllables, ending in -rih-thum. Note the *th* spelling, unlike *logarithm*'s cousin *rhythm*.

gloss: A short program that automates a task.
examples: I wrote a *script* to rename all the files.
These *scripts* run every night at two.
The backup *script* failed silently.

gloss: A named block of code that does one job and can be reused.
examples: Pull that logic out into its own *function*.
The file has about forty *functions* in it.
The *function* returns an empty list if nothing matches.

gloss: A named place in a program where a value is stored.
examples: Give the *variable* a name that means something.
All these *variables* are global, which is asking for trouble.
The *variable* was never initialized.

gloss: An ordered list of values stored under one name.
examples: Loop through the *array* and print each name.
You can nest *arrays* inside each other.
The *array* starts at index zero.

gloss: A piece of text handled as a single value by a program.
examples: Wrap the *string* in quotation marks.
Compare the two *strings* before you save.
The date is stored as a *string*, not a number.

gloss: The rules for how code or sentences must be written.
examples: The *syntax* is a little different in this language.
One missing bracket and the *syntax* breaks.
It's a *syntax* error on line twelve.

gloss: A program that turns human-written code into something a machine can run.
examples: The *compiler* caught the mistake right away.
Different *compilers* give different warnings.
The *compiler* takes about a minute on this machine.

gloss: A collection of ready-made code that other programs can use.
examples: There's a *library* that already does that.
The project depends on about sixty *libraries*.
That *library* hasn't been updated in years.
contrast: Three syllables in careful American speech: LY-brair-ee. "LY-berry" is common but considered sloppy.

gloss: A ready-made structure that programs are built on top of.
examples: They rebuilt the site on a modern *framework*.
New *frameworks* come out every six months.
The *framework* handles all the routing for you.

gloss: An instruction typed in to make a computer do something.
examples: Type the *command* exactly as it's written.
I never remember the *commands* for that tool.
One *command* wipes the whole folder, so be careful.

gloss: The text you type to tell a program or an AI model what you want.
examples: A clearer *prompt* gets a much better answer.
He keeps a file of *prompts* he reuses.
The *prompt* was too vague, so the output was too.

gloss: Information put into a computer for it to work on.
examples: The program waits for *input* from the keyboard.
Bad *input* gives you bad results.
It takes plain text as *input*.

gloss: What a computer or program produces after it processes something.
examples: Save the *output* to a file.
The *output* was full of warnings.
Compare the *output* against the sample.

gloss: A mistake that stops a program from working correctly.
examples: I got an *error* when I tried to save.
The log is full of the same *errors*.
The *error* message wasn't very helpful.

gloss: A small, usually brief fault in a system.
examples: It was just a *glitch* — it works now.
There were a few *glitches* on launch day.
A *glitch* in the app charged me twice.

gloss: A store of data kept nearby so it can be fetched again quickly.
examples: Clear your *cache* and try again.
The *caches* fill up over time.
The page is being served from the *cache*.
contrast: Pronounced exactly like *cash*. It is not "ka-SHAY" — that is the separate word *cachet*.

gloss: A delay between an action and the system's response.
examples: There's a lot of *lag* on this connection.
The *lag* makes the game unplayable.
A little *lag* on video calls is normal.

gloss: Facts and figures stored or processed by a computer.
examples: We lost three days of *data*.
The *data* shows a clear pattern.
They sell your *data* to advertisers.
contrast: Treated as uncountable in everyday American English: *the data is clear*. The old Latin singular *datum* survives only in formal writing.

gloss: An organized store of information a computer can search.
examples: Everything goes into one *database*.
The two *databases* don't talk to each other.
The *database* has about four million rows.

gloss: A basic unit of computer storage, made of eight bits.
examples: One character takes up about a *byte*.
The file is only nine hundred *bytes*.
Every *byte* counts on a device that small.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *bite*. The spelling with *y* keeps the two words apart in writing.

gloss: A unit of storage equal to about a billion bytes.
examples: The movie is four *gigabytes*.
My plan gives me twenty *gigabytes* a month.
One *gigabyte* doesn't go very far anymore.
contrast: Both g's are hard, as in *give*: GIG-uh-byte, never "JIG-uh-byte."

gloss: Space on a device or online where files are kept.
examples: I'm out of *storage* on my phone.
Cloud *storage* is cheap now.
The laptop comes with a terabyte of *storage*.

gloss: A device that stores data, or a piece of storage the computer treats as one unit.
examples: Back everything up to an external *drive*.
The server has eight *drives* in it.
The *drive* died without any warning.

gloss: The main storage device inside a computer.
examples: The *hard drive* is almost full.
Old *hard drives* make a clicking noise before they fail.
I replaced the *hard drive* with a faster one.

gloss: A flat piece of storage that a computer reads and writes data on.
examples: The *disk* is running out of space.
Both *disks* are mirrored, so nothing is lost.
Copy the file to the *disk* first.
contrast: American computing uses *disk* with a k; *disc* with a c is for music and movies — a compact disc.

gloss: A spare copy of files kept in case the original is lost.
examples: Luckily we had a *backup* from Friday.
The *backups* run automatically overnight.
Make a *backup* before you upgrade.
contrast: One word as a noun (*a backup*), two words as a verb (*back up your files*).

gloss: A computer built to sit on a desk rather than be carried around.
examples: He does all his editing on a *desktop*.
The office still runs on *desktops*.
A *desktop* gives you more power for the money than a laptop.

gloss: A device for talking to someone at a distance, now usually a handheld one.
examples: My *phone* died in the middle of the call.
Please put your *phones* away during the exam.
She left her *phone* in the car.

gloss: A phone that also runs apps and connects to the internet.
examples: Almost everyone here has a *smartphone*.
New *smartphones* come out every fall.
The camera on that *smartphone* is better than my old one.

gloss: A phone that works over a wireless network instead of a wire.
examples: Give me a call on my *cellphone*.
*Cellphones* aren't allowed on the factory floor.
There's no *cellphone* service in the mountains.
contrast: Americans say *cellphone* or just *cell*; British speakers say *mobile* or *mobile phone*.

gloss: A watch that runs apps and connects to your phone.
examples: His *smartwatch* tracks his heart rate.
*Smartwatches* have to be charged almost every night.
I got a *smartwatch* for my birthday.

gloss: A device that takes photographs or video.
examples: The *camera* on this phone is incredible.
There are security *cameras* at every entrance.
Turn your *camera* on so we can see you.

gloss: A small camera used for video calls and streaming.
examples: My *webcam* stopped working before the interview.
Cheap *webcams* look terrible in low light.
Cover the *webcam* when you're not using it.

gloss: A device that turns an electrical signal into sound.
examples: The *speaker* on my laptop is tinny.
He hooked up a pair of *speakers* in the garage.
Put it on *speaker* so everyone can hear.

gloss: A device that picks up sound and turns it into a signal.
examples: Your *microphone* is muted.
They set up two *microphones* on the stage.
Speak a little closer to the *microphone*.

gloss: Headphones with a microphone attached, worn over the head.
examples: Support staff wear a *headset* all day.
The company bought new *headsets* for everyone.
My *headset* cuts out every few minutes.

gloss: Small headphones that sit inside the ear.
examples: I lost one of my *earbuds* on the bus.
These *earbuds* last about six hours on a charge.
He had *earbuds* in and didn't hear me.

gloss: A machine that turns a paper document or photo into a computer file.
examples: Put the form in the *scanner* face down.
The library has two *scanners* by the front desk.
The *scanner* jammed on the third page.

gloss: A small device or program that does arithmetic.
examples: You can't use a *calculator* on this section of the test.
The store sells graphing *calculators* for eighty dollars.
There's a *calculator* built into your phone.

gloss: An aircraft flown with no pilot on board.
examples: A *drone* filmed the whole wedding from above.
*Drones* are banned within five miles of the airport.
He crashed his *drone* into a tree.

gloss: A machine that can carry out tasks on its own.
examples: A *robot* welds the doors on the assembly line.
The warehouse uses *robots* to move the shelves around.
We have a little *robot* that vacuums the floor.

gloss: A device that detects light, heat, movement, or another condition.
examples: The *sensor* turns the lights on when you walk in.
The car is covered in *sensors*.
A dirty *sensor* gives you a false reading.

gloss: A device that makes a narrow, very strong beam of light.
examples: The *laser* cuts through steel like paper.
Surgeons use *lasers* for that procedure now.
A *laser* reads the code at the checkout.

gloss: A screen you control by touching it with your fingers.
examples: The *touchscreen* in the car is hard to use while driving.
*Touchscreens* don't work well with gloves on.
The *touchscreen* stopped responding in the cold.

gloss: The screen that shows what a device is doing.
examples: The *display* is bright enough to read in the sun.
He runs three *displays* on his desk.
The *display* cracked when I dropped it.

gloss: The chip that does the main work inside a computer.
examples: The new *processor* is twice as fast.
These *processors* run hot under load.
A faster *processor* won't help if you're short on memory.

gloss: A tiny piece of silicon holding an electronic circuit.
examples: There's a *microchip* in every credit card now.
The shortage of *microchips* shut down car factories.
The vet put a *microchip* in the dog.

gloss: The main circuit board that everything else in a computer plugs into.
examples: The *motherboard* is fried.
These *motherboards* have four memory slots.
Replacing the *motherboard* costs almost as much as a new machine.

gloss: A tiny electronic part that switches or strengthens a signal.
examples: A modern chip holds billions of *transistors*.
One burned-out *transistor* killed the whole board.
The *transistor* replaced the vacuum tube.

gloss: A closed path that electricity flows around.
examples: The *circuit* trips whenever we run the heater.
He tests *circuits* for a living.
A broken wire opens the *circuit*.
contrast: The *ui* is just a short *i*: SUR-kit, rhyming with *work it*.

gloss: A material that conducts electricity only under certain conditions, used to make chips.
examples: Silicon is the most common *semiconductor*.
*Semiconductors* are made in enormous clean rooms.
The *semiconductor* industry is worth hundreds of billions.

gloss: The element that computer chips are made from.
examples: Chips are cut from a wafer of *silicon*.
*Silicon* is the second most common element in the earth's crust.
They melt sand to get pure *silicon*.
contrast: Do not confuse with *silicone*, the rubbery sealant, which ends in an extra *e* and a long *ohn* sound.

gloss: A small part that lets one kind of plug or device work with another.
examples: You'll need an *adapter* for European outlets.
I keep a drawer full of *adapters*.
The laptop came with a power *adapter*.
contrast: Americans usually spell it *adapter*; the spelling *adaptor* is more common in Britain.

gloss: A socket on a device where a cable plugs in.
examples: Plug the drive into the *port* on the left.
The laptop only has two *ports*.
The charging *port* is full of lint.

gloss: A device that gives you several extra ports from one connection.
examples: I plug everything into one *hub*.
Cheap *hubs* can't supply enough power.
The *hub* gives me four extra USB ports.

gloss: The box that connects your home network to your internet provider.
examples: Unplug the *modem* for ten seconds and plug it back in.
The company rents *modems* for ten dollars a month.
The *modem* has been blinking red all morning.

gloss: A small container that slides into a machine, such as one holding printer ink.
examples: The black *cartridge* is empty again.
Replacement *cartridges* cost more than the printer did.
Shake the *cartridge* before you put it in.

gloss: A handheld device used to control a game or machine.
examples: The *controller* needs new batteries.
We only have two *controllers*, so somebody has to sit out.
He threw the *controller* across the room.

gloss: A small clever device that does one particular job.
examples: He buys every new *gadget* that comes out.
The kitchen drawer is full of *gadgets* we never use.
It's a handy little *gadget* for opening jars.

gloss: A machine that turns fuel or electricity into movement.
examples: The *engine* wouldn't start this morning.
Jet *engines* are tested for thousands of hours.
Listen to the *engine* when you're idling.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The set you watch programs on, or the medium of broadcasting itself.
examples: They bought a bigger *television* for the basement.
The store had forty *televisions* on the wall.
He works in *television*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Scientific knowledge used to make machines and tools, or one particular such method.
examples: *Technology* changes faster than the law does.
Two new *technologies* came out of that lab.
The hospital invested in imaging *technology*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The making of new things or methods, or a new thing itself.
examples: The company is known for *innovation*.
The last decade brought a few real *innovations*.
Their biggest *innovation* was the touch interface.

gloss: Something new that someone has made for the first time.
examples: The wheel is the classic example of an *invention*.
Most of his *inventions* never made it to market.
Her *invention* cuts the process from an hour to five minutes.

gloss: The use of science to design and build machines, structures, and systems.
examples: She studied electrical *engineering*.
The bridge is a marvel of *engineering*.
*Engineering* jobs are in demand right now.

gloss: The first working model of something, built to test the idea.
examples: They built a *prototype* out of cardboard and tape.
The first two *prototypes* both failed.
The *prototype* is nowhere near ready to sell.

gloss: A detailed technical drawing showing how something is to be built.
examples: The *blueprint* is spread out on the table.
The city keeps *blueprints* of every building downtown.
The wiring doesn't match the *blueprint*.

gloss: A legal right that stops others from copying an invention.
examples: They filed a *patent* on the design.
The company holds thousands of *patents*.
The *patent* runs out in three years.
contrast: Americans say PAT-unt with a short *a*; British speakers usually say PAY-tunt.

gloss: A room fitted out for scientific work or testing.
examples: The sample went to the *laboratory* on Monday.
The university has six research *laboratories*.
No food or drink in the *laboratory*.
contrast: American stress is on the first syllable, LAB-ruh-tor-ee; the British say luh-BOR-uh-tree.

gloss: The use of machines and software to do work people used to do.
examples: *Automation* cut the crew from twelve people to three.
The plant runs almost entirely on *automation*.
*Automation* is coming for a lot of office work.

gloss: The branch of engineering that deals with building robots.
examples: *Robotics* is her field.
The high school has a *robotics* club.
*Robotics* has changed manufacturing completely.
contrast: Like *physics* and *economics*, it takes a singular verb: *robotics is*, not *robotics are*.

gloss: A set of parts working together as a whole.
examples: The whole *system* went down for two hours.
The two *systems* don't share data.
Log in to the *system* with your work account.

gloss: One of the parts that something larger is made of.
examples: The failed *component* costs four dollars.
Most of the *components* are made overseas.
Every *component* is tested before it ships.

gloss: A self-contained part that fits together with others to make a whole.
examples: Each *module* can be replaced on its own.
The course is split into six *modules*.
The memory *module* wasn't seated properly.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The act of putting equipment or software in place, or a system that has been put in place.
examples: *Installation* takes about ten minutes.
They handle *installations* all over the state.
The *installation* failed halfway through.

gloss: The work of keeping equipment in good working order.
examples: The site is down for scheduled *maintenance*.
Regular *maintenance* keeps the machines running.
*Maintenance* costs more than we budgeted.
contrast: Spelled *maintenance*, not "maintainance" — the verb *maintain* loses its *ai* in the noun.

gloss: The way equipment is arranged and configured, or the process of arranging it.
examples: His home office *setup* cost more than his car.
Both *setups* use the same software.
*Setup* took about twenty minutes.
contrast: One word as a noun (*a setup*), two words as a verb (*set up the printer*).

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The number of times a wave repeats each second, or how often something happens.
examples: The radio broadcasts on a low *frequency*.
Emergency crews use their own *frequencies*.
Higher *frequency* means shorter range.
